              v.                                     )       Case No. 26-cv-1208
                                                     )
RURAL MEDIA GROUP, INC.,                             )
                                                     )
              Defendant.                             )

                                   ORDER AND OPINION

       Plaintiff Illinois Agricultural Association (“IAA”) has filed a Motion for Preliminary

Injunction against Defendant Rural Media Group, Inc. (“RMG”). (D. 13). Evidentiary hearings on

that Motion were held on September 3 and 9, 2026. Closing arguments were heard on September

23, 2026. For the reasons set forth below, IAA’s [13] Motion is GRANTED.

                                    I.      INTRODUCTION

       This is now the second trademark infringement case IAA has filed against RMG stemming

from RMG’s use of IAA’s “RFD” trademarks. See Illinois Agricultural Assoc. v. Rural Media

Group, Inc. et al, CDIL Case No. 13-cv-1220 (“2013 Case”). These cases stem from IAA’s Federal

Trademark Registrations for “RFD” (U.S. Reg. Nos. 3,404,674 and 3,404,675) and “RFD Radio

Network and design” (U.S. Reg. Nos. 3,404,671 and 3,404,672) (collectively, “RFD Marks”),

which they have owned since April 1, 2008. See (D. 1-1; D. 1-2; D. 1-3; D. 1-4). IAA’s RFD

Marks are for “audio broadcasting, in Class 38” and “education and entertainment services,

namely, a continuing program about news, markets, weather and feature reports accessible by

radio, audio, and computer networks, in Class 41.” See id.




                                                 1
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50       Filed: 10/05/26    Page 2 of 23




       IAA’s 2013 Case stemmed from IAA’s RFD Marks, RMG’s unsuccessful attempts to

acquire the RFD Marks from IAA, and then RMG proceeding to issue press release in May 2013

announcing its launch of SiriusXM radio channel to be called “Radio RFD.” IAA’s complaint

alleged this violated its trademark rights and threatened consumer confusion in the agricultural

broadcasting market and sought a preliminary injunction. Before ruling of IAA’s motion for

preliminary injunction, IAA and RMG entered a “Stipulation and Order” in June 2013. (2013 Case,

D. 31 (“2013 Order”)). The 2013 Order established that that that RMG would not:

       announce, advertise, promote, launch, disseminate, provide or broadcast a radio
       channel, station or broadcasting service, or programming and content therefor,
       whether through radio media or other means of transmitting radio programming
       including the internet, under the “Radio RFD” name, or any name, mark, call-sign
       or other source identifier that is confusingly similar to any of IAA’s RFD Marks.

Id. at p. 1. The 2013 Order permitted RMG to continue using its pre-existing “RFD-TV” Marks

(namely, RFD-TV, RFD-TV THE MAGAZINE, and RFD-TV THE THEATRE), even on radio,

as long as the RFD-TV Marks were not used in the name of the radio channel or radio channel

programming. Id. The Order also prohibits RMG from using the “RFD-TV” Marks “in connection

with the radio channel that is likely to cause confusion regarding the name, source or sponsorship

of the radio channel (e.g., by referring to the radio channel as RFD-TV’s Rural radio channel).”

Id. at pp. 1–2. Following the 2013 Order, RMG renamed its SiriusXM radio channel “Rural

Radio.”

       Presently before this Court is IAA’s trademark infringement case against RMG, which

stems from RMG’s public announcement on January 26, 2026, that it was “transitioning from

Rural Media Group to RFD Network” and that “RFD Network now unifies its core platforms—

RFD-TV (linear), RFD+ (streaming), Rural Radio on SiriusXM, podcasts, and digital properties—




                                                  2
             1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH                  # 50       Filed: 10/05/26         Page 3 of 23




under a single network brand.” (D. 1-5; D. 17, ¶¶ 33–34). Like before, this announcement came

after RMG attempted and failed to acquire rights to IAA’s RFD Marks.

        In addition to IAA’s RFD Marks and prior lawsuit, the following history of the parties’

operations provides the background of this lawsuit.

                                            II.      BACKGROUND1

    A. IAA:

        IAA is a non-profit corporation founded in 1916 to champion farmers’ interests through

education, non-partisan lobbying and legislative advocacy, and community support. IAA is a

membership-organization comprised of 92 county organizations and governed by a 20-member

board that meets monthly in Bloomington, Illinois. It is one of the first farm bureaus in the country

and operates under the tradename “Illinois Farm Bureau.” IAA established RFD Radio in 1967. It

was initially called “Rural Free Delivery,” which was later shortened to the acronym “RFD.” Over

the last sixty years, IAA has continuously produced and broadcasted radio programming under the

marks “RFD,” “RFD Illinois,” and now “RFD Radio Network.”2 RFD Radio Network is one of

IAA’s most important means for educating and informing its listeners on the latest news in

agriculture.

        Today, RFD Radio Network has over eighty radio station affiliates that broadcast

throughout Illinois, with spillover into neighboring states (e.g. Iowa, Indiana, and Missouri) who

utilize RFD Radio Network’s information on their broadcasts. (See D. 30, pp. 24, 59). IAA target

audience is primarily their members, listeners at affiliate stations, and rural America. Since 1967,

IAA’s RFD-branded programing has expanded overtime to include RFD Today (1995–present),


1
  IAA’s and RMG’s background information is based on the exhibits and testimony provided at the September 3,
2026, evidentiary hearing. (D. 30). At that hearing, Phillip Nelson, current IAA president, and Gatsby Gottsch
Solheim, part-owner and chief financial and legal officer at RMG, both testified regarding the parties’ backgrounds.
2
  RFD Radio Network was used in a publication in 1994, and IAA still uses this name today. (D. 30, p. 30).

                                                          3
            1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50        Filed: 10/05/26     Page 4 of 23




RFD Livestock Report (2004–present), Best of RFD (2018–present), RFD Profit Watch (2019–

present), RFD Vintage Country (2023–present), and RFD Town and Country Partners (2018–

2023). RFD Radio Network’s programming is also available online for on-demand streaming

throughout     the     United     States    and        worldwide     at    www.FarmWeekNow.com

(www.farmweeknow.com/rfd_radio).

       IAA filed applications with the USPTO for “RFD” and “RFD Radio Network” in June

2007, reflecting first use in 1967. These trademarks have been registered to IAA since April 1,

2008. Below is RFD Radio Network’s registered trademarked design, which is displayed at the

top of Farm Week Now’s website:




       Users that click on the RFD Radio Network link are taken to the homepage for RFD Radio

Network      Content   where     its   various    programs     can    be   streamed    on   demand.

https://www.farmweeknow.com/rfd_radio/ (last visited 09/22/2026). The top of this page states,

“RFD Radio Network™ is the most listened to source for Illinois agriculture news and

information. Listen on your favorite radio station that carries RFD Radio Network.” Id. In addition

to being able to stream RFD Radio Network, there are also separate links to stream on-demand

segments from “RFD Illinois,” “RFD Profit Watch,” “Livestock Report,” “Best of RFD,” “Vintage

Country,” and a link to its “Talking Stalk Podcast with Illinois Farm Bureau.” Id. There are also

links to additional content created by RFD Radio Network, which includes coverage of all major

events that impact agriculture, including those outside of Illinois. See id.; (D. 30, pp. 38–40).

   B. RMG:

                                                   4
                1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH                 # 50       Filed: 10/05/26          Page 5 of 23




           RMG is a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business currently located in

Nashville, Tennessee. (D. 17, ¶¶ 2–3). In 1988 Patrick Gottsch, along with other family members,

attempted to launch RFD-TV, a Nebraska television network focused on the needs and interests of

agriculture and rural America. RFD-TV was not financially viable, and this attempt ended in

bankruptcy in 1989.3 For next 12–13 years, RFD-TV was not in use while Gottsch looked for

investors. In December 2000, RFD-TV relaunched as a non-profit and was given a channel on the

Dish Network. Around that same time RFD-TV magazine was also launched as a subscription

business serving as a TV guide for the network and included stories about rural lifestyle, culture,

and news. Gottsch also opened RFD-TV Theatre in Branson, Missouri (in the Ray Stevens Theater

facility) around 2007 as a complimentary entertainment business.

           In 2007, Gottsch converted RFD-TV to RMG, a for-profit company. RMG subsequently

hired Don Imus to air his show on RFD-TV after Imus was let go from MSNBC for racist

comments. Imus was last affiliated with RFD-TV in 2009. While the specific dates are not clear,

RFD-TV expanded from the Dish Network to other network providers. These included DirecTV,

Mediacom cable, and other affiliates. Ms. Solheim, Patrick Gottsch’s daughter, testified that RFD-

TV was available in 30 million homes, but no evidence as to the number of viewers was provided.

           Solheim also testified that there was a high-definition version of RFD-TV on those affiliate

networks called RFD HD. She could not recall the exact dates RFD HD was used (thinking it was

sometime between 2008 and 2014 or 2016), and she did not identify any of the affiliate networks

that used RFD HD. She did, however, recall that there had been an application to register RFD

HD. The USPTO denied RMG’s application for the RFD HD mark due to a likelihood of confusion

with IAA’s RFD Marks.



3
    No evidence has been provided that any cable network carried the station during this time.

                                                            5
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50       Filed: 10/05/26    Page 6 of 23




       In 2012, Patrick Gottsch approached IAA about buying or licensing the RFD Marks. IAA

declined. Despite IAA’s refusal, RMG proceeded with launching the Radio RFD channel on

SiriusXM. This led to IAA filing the 2013 Case to enjoin RMG’s use of an allegedly confusing

similar mark on SiriusXM Radio. Shortly after the 2013 Case was filed, the stipulated 2013 Order

set forth above was entered under which RMG agreed that it would “not announce, advertise,

promote, launch, disseminate, provide or broadcast a radio channel, station or broadcasting

service… under the ‘Radio RFD’ name, or any name, mark, call-sign or other source identifier that

is confusingly similar to any of IAA’s RFD Marks.” (2013 Case, D. 31). IAA also agreed that

RMG could continue to use its RFD-TV marks in accordance with the terms of that Order. Id. In

December 2014, the IAA and RMG entered into a confidential settlement agreement making the

2013 Order permanent.

       Following the 2013 case, RMG then renamed its SiriusXM radio channel “Rural Radio,”

which it continues to use. In 2014, RMG launched a digital subscription streaming service for live

and on-demand programming called “The Country Club,” because not every household had access

to RFD-TV at this time. (D. 30, p. 95). In 2020, the Country Club was rebranded as RFD-TV Now,

with an app rebuilding work occurring around the same time as RMG launched another streaming

service for its sister network, the Cowboy Channel.

       In May 2024, Pat Gottsch passed away and his three daughters now own RMG. Prior to

passing, Gottsch entered into an agreement to sell the Cowboy Channel. The acquisition of the

Cowboy Channel closed in November 2024, and included a six-month Transition Service

Agreement, requiring RMG to continue providing essential operational support to the new buyer

until May 2025.




                                                  6
            1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50       Filed: 10/05/26     Page 7 of 23




       In June 2025, RMG hired brand consultant Culture Key to help plan and design a rebrand

of RMG’s different offerings under one “branded house.” (D. 30, p. 102). Ultimately, they decided

to replace RMG with “RFD Network” as the umbrella name. Id. at 164. Under the RFD Network,

RMG included RFD-TV and Rural Radio, rebranded RFD-TV Now as RFD+, and added RFD

Studios, RFD News, and RFD Originals as new marks. Id. Ms. Solheim testified that “[t]he intent

behind rebranding [RMG] to RFD Network was to…signal to the business community primarily,

like our advertisers and others, that these are a connected family of brands.” Id. at 161.

        Below are RMG’s brand design before January 2026, and rebranded design as the RFD

Network, which launched on January 26, 2026:




(RMG’s Pre-January 2026 Branding).




 RFD News                       RFD Originals                            RFD Studios
(RMG’s post-January 26, 2026, RFD Network Branding).



                                                   7
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH          # 50       Filed: 10/05/26   Page 8 of 23




       During the rebranding process RMG was aware of IAA’s RFD Marks and the 2013 Order,

which is why they did not change the name of Rural Radio, despite their brand consultant’s

suggestion to do so. RMG also reached out to IAA in July 2025 seeking to open up discussions

about licensing and/or purchasing the RFD Mark in connection with their rebranding. On

September 18, 2025, IAA declined to allow use of the RFD Marks. On January 24, 2026, RMG

filed an application with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (“USPTO”) to register

“RFD Network.” RMG also submitted applications to register “RFD-TV,” “RFD+,” “RFD News,”

“RFD Studio,” and “RFD Originals.”

       On January 26, 2026, RMG issued a press release titled “RFD NETWORK ENTERS A NEW

CHAPTER WITH MODERNIZED BRAND AND CONTENT-FIRST, MUILTI-PLATFORM

STRATEGY” announcing that it was formally transitioning from “Rural Media Group” to “RFD

Network” which unifies its core platforms—RFD TV, RFD+ (streaming), Rural Radio SiriusXM,

podcasts, and digital properties—under a single network brand.” (D. 1-5; D. 14-15). The press

release could be found on RMG’s website, http://www.rfdtv.com, which remained the same both

before and after rebranding to RFD Network. The press release also announced that RFD-TV Now

was transitioning to RFD+, and that “RFD Network would be expanding its original programming

through RFD Studio, the home of RFD Originals.” Id. It also stated that “RFD Network continues

to be anchored by RFD News, the umbrella for its live news and market coverage.” Id.

       On May 26, 2026, the USPTO issue a Non-Final Office Action, “Section 2(d) Refusal—

Likelihood of Confusion” in response RMG’s application for registration of “RFD Network” mark

“because of a likelihood of confusion with marks in U.S. Registration Nos. 3404675 [IAA’s

“RFD” Service Mark], 1158438 [IAA’s “RFD Illinois” Service Mark], and 3404672 [IAA’s “RFD

Radio Network” Service Mark]. When comparing the “RFD Network” mark to IAA’s RFD Marks,



                                                8
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50       Filed: 10/05/26    Page 9 of 23




the USPO found that the “marks are nearly identical in appearance, sound, commercial impression

and connotation.” Specifically, IAA’s “RFD” and “RFD Illinois” Marks and RMG’s applicant

mark “share[d] the similar fundamental element of ‘RFD’ for related services” and that IAA’s

“RFD Radio Network” Mark shared “similar, fundamental element[s] of ‘RFD’ and ‘NETWORK’

for related services,” to RMG’s “RFD Network” mark. RMG has received the same Non-Final

Office Action, “Section 2(d) Refusal—Likelihood of Confusion” for its applications to register

“RFD-TV,” “RFD+,” “RFD News,” “RFD Studios,” and “RFD Originals.”

       RMG has not yet responded to this non-final office action. It intends to do so. Because the

action by the USPTO is not final and RMG has not yet had the opportunity to respond the weight

of the USPTO’s findings is, although not without value, certainly limited.

   C. This Lawsuit:

       On May 19, 2026, IAA filed this lawsuit against RMG federal trademark infringement

under 15 U.S.C. § 1114, false designation and federal common law trademark infringement under

15 U.S.C. § 1125(a). IAA also brings state law claims against RMG alleging violations of the

Illinois Consumer Fraud and Deceptive Practices Act, 815 ILCS 505/2, Illinois Uniform Deceptive

Trade Practices Act, 815 ILCS 510/2, unfair competition, and breach of contract based on the 2013

Order. (D. 1). IAA subsequently filed a Motion for Preliminary Injunction asking this Court to

preliminarily enjoin RMG from using “RFD Network,” “RFD+,” “RFD News,” “RFD Studios,”

and “RFD Originals” during the pendency of this lawsuit as they violate IAA’s trademark rights.

(D. 13; D. 14). RMG filed a Memorandum in Opposition. (D. 28).

       Two evidentiary hearings were held on September 3rd and 9th on IAA’s Motion for

Preliminary Injunction. (D. 30; D. 38). Phillip Nelson, IAA president; Gatsby Gottscha Solheim,

RMG’s part-owner and chief financial and legal officer; and Adam Weiner, RMG employee,



                                                  9
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50        Filed: 10/05/26     Page 10 of 23




testified at the September 3rd hearing. (D. 30). Expert witness testimony from Dr. David Neal, on

behalf of IAA, and Hal Poret, on behalf of RMG, was heard on September 9th. (D. 38). Ms.

Solheim also testified at the September 9th hearing. See id. at pp. 125–45. Closing arguments were

heard on September 23rd. This Order follows.

                      III.    PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION STANDARD

       Earlier this year, the Seventh Circuit provided the following legal standard for granting a

preliminary injunction in a trademark case:

       A district court may grant a preliminary injunction where the “movant shows that
       it is likely to succeed on the merits of its claims and that traditional legal remedies
       would be inadequate, such that it would suffer irreparable harm without injunctive
       relief.” Grubhub Inc. v. Relish Labs LLC, 80 F.4th 835, 843 (7th Cir. 2023) (citing
       Life Spine, Inc. v. Aegis Spine, Inc., 8 F.4th 531, 539 (7th Cir. 2021)). Trademark
       law affords a rebuttable presumption of irreparable harm to movants who show they
       are likely to succeed on the merits of their trademark infringement claims. Id.; §
       1116(a). If the movant shows it is likely to succeed on the merits, the court next
       “weighs the harm of denying an injunction to the movant against the harm of
       granting an injunction to the nonmovant.” Grubhub, 80 F.4th at 844. The court also
       considers the public interest in granting versus denying the preliminary injunction
       request. Life Spine, 8 F.4th at 539.

Illinois Tamale Co., Inc. v. LC Trademarks, Inc., 164 F.4th 648, 655 (7th Cir. 2026). Because a

preliminary injunction is an extraordinary remedy, to succeed IAA “‘need not show that it

definitely will win the case,’ but it ‘must demonstrate at a minimum how it proposes to prove the

key elements of its case.’” See id. (quoting Grubhub Inc., 80 F.4th at 843); see also Life Spine, 8

F.4th at 540) (distinguishing this as more demanding than a “better than negligible chance”). Under

trademark law, “once the movant establishes a likelihood of success on the merits, it is statutorily

entitled to a rebuttable presumption of irreparable harm.” Grubhub Inc., 80 F.4th at 844 (citing 15

U.S.C. § 1116(c)).

                                        IV.     DISCUSSION

   A. Lanham Act—Trademark Infringement:

                                                  10
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH             # 50        Filed: 10/05/26    Page 11 of 23




       The Lanham Act, which is the core federal trademark statute, defines “trademark” as “any

word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof” that is used “to identify and

distinguish his or her goods…from those manufactured or sold by others and to indicate the source

of the goods.” 15 U.S.C. § 1127. To protect marks, the Lanham Act sets up a voluntary registration

system where the mark owner may apply to the USPTO to have its mark placed on the federal

register. See Jack Daniel’s Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC, 599 U.S. 140, 145–46, 143 S.Ct.

1578, 216 L.Ed.2d 161 (2023). The lead criterion for registration is that the mark serves as a

“trademark to identify and distinguish goods.” Id. at 146 (citing 3 McCarthy § 19:10 (listing the

principal register's eligibility standards)). If it does and all other criteria are met, the “the

registering trademark owner receives certain benefits, useful in infringement litigation.” Id. (citing

Iancu v. Brunetti, 588 U.S. 388, 391, 139 S.Ct. 2294, 204 L.Ed.2d 714 (2019) (noting registration

is prima facie evidence of the mark’s validity)).

       The Lanham Act also provides a federal cause of action for trademark infringement, see

15 U.S.C. §§ 1114 and 1125(a), which IAA has invoked here. See Abitron Austria GmbH v.

Hetronic International, Inc., 600 U.S. 412, 143 S.Ct. 2522, 216 L.Ed.2d 1013 (2023) (noting §§

1114(a) and 1125(a)(1) both prohibit “unauthorized use in commerce of a protected trademark

when, …that use is likely to cause confusion”). To prevail on either claim, IAA must show that:

(1) it owns a valid, protectable trademark, and (2) that RMG’s use of the mark is likely to cause

confusion among consumers. See Grubhub, 80 F.4th at 844.

        It is undisputed that IAA’s RFD Marks are valid, protectable trademarks. Because IAA

registered RFD and RFD Radio Network in 2008, and RFD Illinois prior to that, and has used the

RFD Marks continuously for over five years, they are incontestable. See 15 U.S.C. § 1065. As a

result, RMG cannot—and does not—argue that the RFD Marks are not protected by the Lanham



                                                   11
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH             # 50        Filed: 10/05/26    Page 12 of 23




Act. RMG does, however, argue that customers are unlikely to be confused by its use of “RFD

Network,” “RFD+,” “RFD News,” “RFD Studios,” and “RFD Originals” names.

   B. Likelihood of Confusion:

       “To decide if there is a likelihood of confusion, [courts] ask whether consumers who might

use either product would likely attribute them to a single source.” Uncommon, LLC v. Spigen, Inc.,

926 F.3d 409, 425 (7th Cir. 2019). The Seventh Circuit generally considers seven factors when

making this decision: “(1) the similarity of the marks in appearance and suggestion; (2) the

similarity of the products; (3) the area and manner of concurrent use; (4) the degree of care likely

to be used by consumers; (5) the strength of the plaintiff's mark; (6) whether any

actual confusion exists; and (7) the defendant's intent to palm off its goods as those of the

plaintiffs.” Ty, Inc. v. Jones Group, Inc., 237 F.3d 891, 898 (7th Cir. 2001). Though no factor is

decisive and the weight given to each factor will vary depending on the facts of the case, “usually

the similarity of the marks, the defendant’s intent, and actual confusion are particularly important.”

Grubhub Inc., 80 F.4th at 843 (quoting AutoZone, Inc. v. Strick, 543 F.3d 923, 929 (7th Cir. 2008).

       1. Similarity of the mark:

       We view the mark as a whole to determine whether two marks are similar. AutoZone, Inc.,

543 F.3d at 929; see also Grubhub Inc., 80 F.4th at 848 (“The commercial impression of a trade-

mark is derived from it as a whole, not from its elements separated and considered in detail.” )

(quoting Estate of P.D. Beckwith, Inc. v. Comm’r of Patents, 252 U.S. 538, 545–46, 40 S.Ct. 414,

64 L.Ed. 705 (1920)). Therefore, we must compare the marks “in light of what happens in the

marketplace and not merely by looking at the two marks side-by-side.” Grubhub Inc., 80 F.4th at

848 (quoting AutoZone, Inc., 543 F.3d at 930); see also Ty Inc., 237 F.3d at 898. Thus, “the test is

not whether the public would confuse the marks, but whether the viewer of an accused mark would



                                                   12
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH             # 50        Filed: 10/05/26      Page 13 of 23




be likely to associate the product or service with which it is connected with the source of products

or services with which an earlier mark is connected.” Grubhub Inc., 80 F.4th at 848 (emphasis in

original) (quoting James Burrough Ltd. v. Sign of Beefeater, Inc., 540 F.2d 266, 275 (7th

Cir.1976)). The court should also “consider whether the customer would believe that the trademark

owner sponsored, endorsed or was otherwise affiliated with the product.” AutoZone, Inc., 543 F.3d

at 930 (quoting Nike, Inc. v. “Just Did It” Enters., 6 F.3d 1225, 1228–29 (7th Cir.1993)).

       Here, IAA has sufficiently demonstrated for preliminary injunction purposes that a

consumer would believe that the marks are connected to the same source. In addition to IAA’s

expert findings, which will be discussed under the “actual confusion” category, the marks are not

just similar but use the same identifying name. Specifically, the distinguishing word of both

parties’ marks is “RFD,” which is the first word in all the marks. “RFD” is IAA’s trademark, and

it has been using that mark since 1967 in connection with radio and broadcasting throughout

Illinois, and more recently for steaming on the internet. In addition to IAA’s RFD Marks (“RFD,”

“RFD Radio Network,” and “RFD Illinois”), it also uses RFD Today and RFD Profit Watch. The

marks RMG seeks to use are “RFD Network,” “RFD+,” “RFD News,” “RFD Studios,” and “RFD

Originals.” All marks include “RFD” followed by a generic word or symbol used in media.

Additionally, both marks are being used for news and/or entertainment purposes, including radio

broadcast and online streaming, aimed at a particular audience. The evidence suggests that there

is not only overlap in the parties’ audiences, but also their advertisers.

       While there are dissimilarities in the designs of the marks and they are portrayed in

different colors, the prominent similarities between the marks are substantial. Moreover, because

radio and online streaming are aural mediums, the sound and use of the mark (rather than how the

mark looks) will more likely determine its similarity to other marks. Therefore, RMG’s use of



                                                   13
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH              # 50        Filed: 10/05/26   Page 14 of 23




“RFD,” which is IAA’s trademark, does not just sound similar but is the same. Moreover, despite

RMG’s insistence that they “went to great lengths to ensure rebranding would not result in

customer confusion as it relates to Rural Radio” relying heavily on the 2013 Order, they ignore

that the 2013 Case was narrowly limited to the radio, and RFD Marks include services beyond

radio and they have used it on other mediums than the radio. Furthermore, Rural Radio now falls

under the RFD Network.

        2. Similarity of the product:

        Like the similarity of the mark factor, the inquiry for comparing whether two products are

similar “is not whether they are interchangeable, but whether ‘the parties’ products are the kind

the public might very well attribute to a single source…” Eli Lilly & Co. v. Natural Answers,

Inc., 233 F.3d 456, 463 (7th Cir.2000) (at risk for overruling on other grounds). “The rights of an

owner of a registered trademark extend to any goods or services that, in the minds of consumers,

might be put out by a single producer.” AutoZone, Inc., 543 F.3d at 931. Therefore, “[a] likelihood

of confusion may exist even if the parties are not in direct competition, or their products and

services are not identical.” Id. (internal citations omitted).

        These two parties are not involved in entirely different markets. Rather the services

provided are commercially related and centered around agriculture, farming, and rural America.

While RMG offers additional entertainment content on a larger scale, historically through

television or magazines, there is evidence that some of that content overlaps. Specifically, when it

comes to the radio and internet streaming regarding news, commodities, weather, and educational

programs directed at farming in Illinois and the Midwest. Considering the similarity of the marks

and the overlap in content provided, IAA has demonstrated that a reasonable customer could

conclude that some services provided by RMG are attributable to IAA.



                                                    14
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50        Filed: 10/05/26    Page 15 of 23




       3. Area and manner of concurrent use:

       The third factor addresses “whether there is a relationship in use, promotion, distribution,

or sales between the goods or services of the parties.” CAE, Inc. v. Clean Air Engineering, Inc.,

267 F.3d 660, 681 (7th Cir. 2001) (quoting Forum Corp. of N. Am. v. Forum, Ltd., 903 F.2d 434,

442 (7th Cir. 1990)) (internal quotations omitted). As stated above, there is evidence that both

parties broadcast their products on the radio, and the 2013 Order prohibits RMG from using “RFD”

on the radio due to the likelihood of confusion, even though IAA doesn’t have a channel on

SiriusXM. Both parties also offer content online. There is also evidence that both parties have

advertised their products in the same magazine, suggesting congruences exist between their

potential customers, at minimum in Illinois.

       4. Degree of care exercised by consumers:

       The fourth factor to consider is degree of care likely to be exercised by customers. This

factor supports IAA’s position. The Seventh Circuit has held that “[t]he more widely accessible

and inexpensive the products and services, the more likely that consumers will exercise a lesser

degree of care and discrimination in their purchases.” AutoZone, Inc., 543 F.3d at 933 (quoting

CAE, Inc., 267 F.3d at 683). Moreover, in the context of radio stations, courts have found that the

degree of care likely exercised by customers listening to the radio is likely not very high as most

people are doing other things while they are listening to the radio. There is also no financial stake

when choosing a radio station. While RMG attempts to differentiate its radio station because it

only offers Rural Radio to paid subscribers on SiriusXM (a subscription-based satellite radio

service), it ignores that it has rebranded to offer its radio broadcast under the “RFD Network,”

which is substantially similar to IAA’s RFD Radio Network.




                                                  15
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH              # 50        Filed: 10/05/26   Page 16 of 23




       For these reasons, the Court finds that this factor tends to support IAA’s assertions

regarding the degree of care radio listeners will exercise and that IAA has demonstrated that the

evidence favors the likelihood of confusion.

       5. Strength of IAA’s mark:

       “The stronger the mark, the more likely it is that encroachment on it will produce

confusion. A mark's strength ordinarily corresponds to its economic and marketing strength.” “The

stronger the mark, the more likely it is that encroachment on it will produce confusion.” Sorensen

v. WD-40 Co., 792 F.2d 712, 726 (7th Cir. 2015); see also AutoZone, Inc., 543 F.3d at 933. The

IAA has produced evidence that it has a strong mark, especially within the state of Illinois. The

IAA has been using the RFD Marks since 1967. Since then, it has expanded from 18 affiliate radio

channels to 92. It has also utilized the internet and online streaming to reach listeners outside of

Illinois. The IAA president further testified that in 2024, RFD Radio Network achieved a 72.6

CUME rating among Illinois Class 1+ farmers, which is the highest of all agricultural radio

networks in Illinois. It has also been recognized by the American Farm Bureau Federation and the

National Association of Farm Broadcasting.

       On the other hand, there currently is no evidence of market strength outside of Illinois.

There is also little evidence provided regarding economic strength. While the IAA president

testified that IAA spends approximately $100,000.00 per year on advertising, evidence supporting

that assertion was not provided. He also testified that IAA made money from advertisers, but

neither the exact amount nor evidence supporting that assertion have been produced. Given the

limited evidence concerning this factor at this stage, the Court cannot determine to what extent it

could contribute to the likelihood of confusion but acknowledges IAA has demonstrated that there

is some evidence to establish this factor.



                                                    16
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH               # 50        Filed: 10/05/26   Page 17 of 23




       6. Evidence of Actual Confusion:

       “Evidence of actual confusion, which can be presented as either direct or survey evidence,

is not essential to the of a likelihood of confusion, but where present it ‘is entitled to substantial

weight.’” Grubhub Inc., 80 F.4th at 852 (quoting CAE, Inc., 267 F.3d at 685. As the fact finder at

the preliminary injunction stage, it is within the district court’s purview to weigh the evidence

submitted by the parties on this issue. Id.

       Here, the IAA president testified that he has “had a couple county presidents that have said,

What’s the difference between RFD Radio Network and RFD Network,” and he had to explain

which content was produced by IAA. (D. 30, pp. 59–60). These conversations have occurred over

the last few months when he saw them at different events. No evidence was provided, however,

regarding the exact number of people or their identity that asked President Nelson about the RFD

Network. Moreover, there is no evidence of consumers’ actual confusion other than Dr. Neal’s

survey. There is also limited evidence regarding how much RMG has marketed itself as RFD

Network in the few months prior to these lawsuits being filed creating the opportunity for actual

confusion among a greater number of people to occur. Therefore, while the Court has no reason to

not believe the IAA President or that IAA members were confused when they saw the RFD

Network mark, based on the lack of evidence currently presented his testimony does little to

establish direct, actual confusion. Grubhub, Inc., 80 F.4th at 852 (“depending on the

circumstances, isolated incidents of actual confusion may be disregarded as de minimis”) (citing

Packman, 267 F.3d at 645 (7th Cir. 2001) (collecting cases)).

       On September 9th this Court heard expert testimony from IAA’s expert Dr. David Neal

and RMG’s expert Hal Poret. Dr. Neal was qualified as an expert in survey methodology and

consumer behavior who was hired by IAA to assess whether RMG’s use of “RFD Network” for



                                                     17
            1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH                 # 50        Filed: 10/05/26        Page 18 of 23




radio offerings likely caused consumers to believe that it was affiliated or approved by IAA. (D.

38, pp. 9–10). Poret is a survey researcher who designs, supervises, analyzes, and reports on

consumer surveys. Id. at p. 68. IAA objection to him testifying as an expert. Id.

         In June 2026, Dr. Neal conducted an online “Squirt-style” confusion survey among U.S.

adults who listen to or intend to listen to rural radio and who use Google to search for such content.

He used the Squirt methodology because consumers encounter the parties’ marks in proximity and

operationalized proximity with Google results for “RFD Radio.” Google searches for “RFD Radio”

showed IAA’s link first, with RMG’s link for RFD-TV second, and additional RMG links in close

proximity on the first page and on subsequent pages. Dr. Neal testified he skipped the RFD-TV

link that appeared second, and other entries referencing RFD-TV on the first google page to keep

the focus on “RFD Network.” He ultimately used links that appeared on the second and third pages

of Google but were limited to “RFD Network” alone for his survey. This was a major source of

criticism by Poret, RMG’s expert.4 In fact, Poret had nothing good to say about Dr. Neal’s

methodology and conclusions, calling them “worthless.”

        While this Court has some reservations concerning Dr. Neal’s selection of certain “foils”

to be used in the survey, the Court finds the methodology and conclusions essentially sound. Dr.

Neal testified that his survey resulted in a finding that 16.3% of consumers,5 who would not

otherwise have been confused, were confused because of RMG’s use of RFD Network. (See D.

38, pp. 22–27 (explaining survey results)). Dr. Neal concluded, holding everything else constant,

RMG’s use of RFD Network “is causing a substantial likelihood of confusion among relevant

RFD Network is still using the old domain name www.rfdtv.com.
5

                                                        18
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50        Filed: 10/05/26   Page 19 of 23




consumers in the context of these Google search results.” Id. at p. 27; see also Nike, Inc. v. “Just

Did It” Enters., 6 F.3d 1225, 1231 (7th Cir. 1993) (citing Burrough Limited v. Sign of Beefeater,

Inc., 540 F.2d 266, 277–79 (7th Cir. 1976) (noting “as a matter of law survey showing 15% of

customers confused evidences a likelihood of customer confusion.”)).

       It may well be at trial that RMG presents a survey contradicting Dr. Neal’s survey; that is

a matter for another day. At this time, however, the Court finds that IAA has presented evidence

showing they are likely to succeed at showing actual confusion.

       7. Intent to palm off:

       The Court does not believe that RMG intended to confuse consumers—ultimately, just did

not care. RMG chose to go forward with this rebrand because that is what they wanted to do,

knowing it would be resisted by IAA. RMG did it anyway. Even in the face of a final rejection

from the USPTO several years prior when they tried to register RFD HD due to the likelihood of

confusion from IAA’s RFD Marks and now followed by non-final rejections from the USPTO of

the RFD marks that are the subject of this litigation.

       Additionally, IAA has provided evidence that its RFD Marks have attained notoriety in the

agricultural industry, especially in Illinois, which is a geographic area where RMG competes. See

Sands, Taylor & Wood Co. v. Quaker Oats Co., 978 F.2d 947, 963 (7th Cir.1992) (holding intent

to confuse may be inferred in some circumstances from the similarity of the Marks where the

senior mark has great notoriety). The Seventh Circuit has held that when “the marketing and

business presence of the senior mark [IAA’s RFD Marks in this case] are nearly ubiquitous in the

geographic area where the junior mark competes, a trier of fact can easily conclude that the creator

of a strikingly similar junior mark intended to confuse.” AutoZone, Inc., 543 F.3d at 943.




                                                  19
               1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH                 # 50        Filed: 10/05/26        Page 20 of 23




Accordingly, IAA has demonstrated that there is evidence supporting likelihood of confusion

under this factor.

           From these findings we conclude that IAA is likely to succeed on the merits of its

infringement claim(s) under the Lanham Act. The evidence clearly establishes a likelihood of

public confusion as to the source of origin of RFD Network, RFD+, RFD News, RFD Studios, and

RFD Original, which is the bedrock for injunctive relief. This is reinforced by IAA’s RFD Marks

being incontestable and the USPTO examining attorney’s initial findings rejecting RMG’s

applications for RFD-formative marks for RFD HD for likelihood of confusion (final decision)

and making an initial rejection under § 2(d) of RMG’s RFD marks in this case.6

       C. Substantial Threat of Irreparable Injury:

           Under 15 U.S.C. § 1116(a), IAA, as a party seeking a preliminary injunction, is entitled to

a rebuttable presumption of irreparable harm upon this Court's finding that it has a likelihood of

success on its trademark infringement claim. See Ill. Tamale Co., 164 F.4th at 654; see also Eli

Lilly & Co., 233 F.3d at 469 (“Irreparable harm is generally presumed in the case of trademark

infringement); see also (7th Cir.2000); Abbott Labs. v. Mead Johnson & Co., 971 F.2d 6, 16 (7th

Cir. 1992) (recognizing the “well-established presumption that injuries arising from Lanham Act

violations are irreparable, even absent a showing of business loss”).

           Here, IAA asserts that not only has RMG failed to rebut the resumption of irreparable harm,

it has independently demonstrated a likelihood of irreparable harm because it cannot control the

nature and quality of goods RMG is offering under confusingly similar marks, IAA has spent over

60 years building the reputation and goodwill associated with its RFD Marks and they are subject

to tarnishment due to association with RMG’s RFD marks over which they have no control, and

                                                           20
           1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH            # 50        Filed: 10/05/26    Page 21 of 23




is heightened due to IAA being “a non-partisan, not-for-profit advocacy organization that carefully

vets its messaging and public interest positions” being associated with RMG’s for-profit

programming. IAA also asserts that loss of goodwill and reputational danger are not readily

quantifiable or compensable in money damages. This Court agrees.

       RMG’s argument that IAA is not entitled to the rebuttable presumption of irreparable harm

under § 1116(a) because they have not demonstrated a strong likelihood of success on the merits

is inconsistent with this Court’s findings above. Moreover, while the Court agrees with RMG that

IAA’s arguments relating to past programs aired by RMG involving controversial figures such as

Don Imus and Paula Dean are not persuasive, it does nothing to address IAA’s loss of control over

the representation and association with its RFD Marks going forward.

   D. Balance of Equities:

       IAA’s argument that any harm to RMG is “self-inflicted” is well taken. RMG argues that

it “reasonably believed that it was complying with the 2013 Order, which was expressly limited to

radio and did not restrict the use of ‘RFD’ without the ‘TV’ suffix in non-radio contexts.” (D. 34,

¶ 49). This asks the Court to ignore that RMG knew that, in addition to the 2013 Order, IAA owned

the trademarks for “RFD” and “RFD Radio Network,” which is evidenced by RMG asking IAA

to purchase or license their RFD Marks and receiving multiple rejections from the USPTO after

they tried to register their RFD marks when IAA declined letting them use them. This is not a case

where the distinguishing letters in the marks are similar, but rather the same.

       Despite knowing all of this—and having admitted that they could have filed for a

declaratory judgment regarding their rights under the 2013 Order—RMG instead decided to go

ahead and spend approximately $620,000.00 to rebrand using RFD, and now asks the Court to




                                                  21
            1:26-cv-01208-MMM-RLH                # 50        Filed: 10/05/26      Page 22 of 23




balance this harm in their favor.7 The Court will not do so. The evidence shows that RMG knew

that IAA owned the RFD Marks. Therefore, RMG had a duty to select a trademark that would

avoid confusion when rebranding. See Wesley-Jessen Div. of Schering Corp. v. Bausch & Lomb

Inc., 698 F.3d 862, 868 (7th Cir. 1983). For these same reasons, RMG “cannot now complain that

having to mend its ways will be too expensive.” Processed Plastic Co. v. Warner Communications,

Inc., 675 F.2d 852, 859 (7th Cir. 1982).

        The Court also finds that the brief time RMG has spent rebranded as the RFD Network

compared to the decades it has spent using its prior names, minimizes any potential harm to RMG

posed by the Court’s preliminary injunction. The injunction is also narrowly tailored to preserve

the status quo during the pendency of this litigation as it only applies to RMG’s use of “RFD

Network,” “RFD+,” “RFD News,” “RFD Studios,” and “RFD Originals.” RMG is free to return

to its prior branding, which includes the use of the RFD-TV marks as set forth in the 2013 Order.

The Court is not forcing RMG to stop providing any of its services. For these reasons, the Court

finds that the hardships set forth by RMG do not warrant denial to preliminary relief to IAA, where

a strong likelihood of success on the merits has been shown and a strong potential for irreparable

injury has been shown.

        The final element for the Court to consider is whether the granting of preliminary relief

will disserve the public interest. See Wesley-Jessen Div. of Schering Corp, 698 F.3d at 868 (“The

question is not whether the public interest will be served, but whether the public interest will be

disserved.”) (emphasis in original). Based on the record currently before this Court and the

findings and conclusions contained in this Order, it is clear that there is a likelihood of confusion,

LLC; and $26,457.50 in legal fees. (D. 34, ¶ 85 (citing D. 28-1, pp. 11–12).

between broadcasts provided under IAA’s RFD Marks and the RFD marks being used by RMG.

See Eli Lilly & Co., 233 F.3d at 469 (“public interest is served by [an] injunction because

enforcement of trademark law prevents consumer confusion”).

         Moreover, RMG’s argument that IAA’s proposed injunction would “deprive millions of

consumers of access to RMG’s television, streaming, and digital services” is unsupported and

unpersuasive. As stated above, RMG can continue to provide these services under the names used

prior to January 2026, including the RFD-TV marks. IAA has met the burden of showing by a

preponderance of the evidence that the public interest will be served by the granting of a

preliminary injunction.

                                      V.     CONCLUSION

         For the reasons stated above, IAA’s [13] Motion for Preliminary Injunction is GRANTED

against Defendant RMG. The Clerk is DIRECTED to separately enter the Preliminary Injunction

Order.

Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS         Document 64     Filed 08/14/26     Page 1 of 8     Page ID #147




                          UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                      FOR THE SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF ILLINOIS

     TYLER HACKETHAL,                          )
                                               )
     Plaintiff,                                )
                                               )
     vs.                                       ) Case No. 3:25-cv-00414-GCS
                                               )
     TIFFANY PHILLIPS, SUSAN                   )
     SCHNIERS, BOBBY PLUM,                     )
                                               )
     Defendants.                               )



                                MEMORANDUM & ORDER

 SISON, Magistrate Judge:

           Plaintiff Tyler Hackethal, an inmate of the Illinois Department of Corrections

 ("IDOC"),1 brings this civil rights action pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for alleged violations

 of his constitutional rights at Pinckneyville Correctional Center (“Pinckneyville”). (Doc.

 1). Pending before the Court is a Motion for Summary Judgment on the Issue of

 Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies by Defendant Tiffany Phillips and joined by

 Defendants Susan Schniers and Bob Blum.2 (Doc. 55, Doc. 61, Doc. 62). For the reasons

 explained below, the Court GRANTS the Motion for Summary Judgment on the Issue of

 Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies.




 1         Hackethal is currently incarcerated at Graham Correctional Center. (Doc. 63)
 2      While Defendant Blum is listed as “Bobby Plum” on the docket, his filings indicate
 that his name is Bob Blum. (Doc. 38, Doc. 41). The Court will refer to him as Bob Blum in
 this Memorandum & Order.

                                          Page 1 of 8
 Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS       Document 64       Filed 08/14/26    Page 2 of 8     Page ID #148




                                PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND

          Plaintiff filed his Complaint on March 27, 2025. (Doc. 1). He alleged that between

 January 9 and January 13, 2025, Plaintiff submitted a medication refill sticker for his blood

 pressure medication. (Doc. 1, p. 3). Nearly a week later, Plaintiff had only one dose left

 and had not received a refill, so he asked the nurse to whom he had submitted the sticker

 about its status. Id. The nurse confirmed that Plaintiff had not received a refill and placed

 him on the medical call list for the next day. Id. Nonetheless, Plaintiff did not receive a

 refill the next day or in the days that followed. Id. Within a few days of running out of

 medication, Plaintiff experienced chest pain, blurry vision, fatigue, and lightheadedness.

 Id. Soon after, Plaintiff explained his symptoms to Defendant Phillips and asked her

 about his prescription. Id. at p. 3-4. Defendant Phillips promised that she would come

 back, but she did not do so. Id. at p. 4. On the same day, Plaintiff told Defendant Schniers

 the same thing that he had told Defendant Phillips, i.e., he was out of medication and

 suffering from symptoms. Id. Defendant Phillips told him to lie down. Id.

         Plaintiff’s symptoms worsened over the next week. (Doc. 1, p. 4). He continued to

 ask Defendants Phillips and Schniers for help, but they did nothing. Id. Ultimately,

 Plaintiff alleges he went fifty-two days without medication. Id. at p. 5. The lapses in

 medication caused him immediate harm and increased his risk of medical harm in the

 future. Id. at p. 6.

         Based on the above allegations, the Court allowed Plaintiff to proceed on the

 following claim:



                                         Page 2 of 8
 Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS        Document 64       Filed 08/14/26    Page 3 of 8     Page ID #149




        Count 1:       Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claim against
                       Jane Does 1-2 and Jane Doe Nurse Practitioner for failing to
                       address Plaintiff’s lack of medication, leaving him without
                       his Lisinopril medication for approximately 52 days from
                       January to March of 2025.

 (Doc. 10, p. 3, 5).

        On February 16, 2026, Defendant Phillips filed a Motion for Summary Judgment

 on the Issue of Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies. (Doc. 55). Plaintiff filed a

 response on March 12, 2026. (Doc. 59). Defendants Schniers and Blum sought to join

 Defendant Phillips’ Motion. (Doc. 56). The Court denied this motion because Defendants

 Schniers and Blum had previously withdrawn the affirmative defense of exhaustion of

 administrative remedies and could not reassert it without moving for leave to file an

 amended answer. (Doc. 49, Doc. 60). Defendants Schniers and Blum subsequently moved

 for leave to file an amended answer and to join Defendant Phillips’s Motion for Summary

 Judgment. (Doc. 61). The Court granted both motions. (Doc. 62). Accordingly, the issue

 of exhaustion is now ripe for the Court’s review.

                                   FACTUAL BACKGROUND

        The parties have limited their discussion of Plaintiff’s grievance record to one

 grievance and its subsequent appeal to the Administrative Review Board (“ARB”). (Doc.

 55, p. 7; Doc. 59, p. 1-2). The Court's discussion is therefore limited to this grievance.

 A.     Grievance No. K59-0225-888

        Plaintiff submitted Grievance No. K59-0225-888 to the Counselor at Pinckneyville

 on February 24, 2025, marking it as an emergency. (Doc. 55-1, p. 4). Plaintiff complained




                                          Page 3 of 8
 Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS         Document 64        Filed 08/14/26    Page 4 of 8     Page ID #150




 that he turned in a refill sticker for his blood pressure medication in early January 2025

 but had not received a refill more than a month later. Id.

          On February 28, 2025, the Chief Administrative Officer (“CAO”) determined that

 the grievance was an emergency and expedited the grievance process. (Doc. 55-1, p. 4).

 On March 17, 2025, a Grievance Officer reviewed the grievance and recommended that

 the grievance be denied. Id. at p. 3. The next day, the CAO concurred with the

 recommendation. Id. Plaintiff then appealed the grievance to the ARB. Id. The ARB

 received Plaintiff’s appeal on March 24, 2025, and denied the appeal three weeks later, on

 April 15, 2025. (Doc. 55-1, p. 2; Doc. 59, p. 1, 4).

                                       LEGAL STANDARDS

          Summary judgment is proper when a moving party cannot establish the presence

 of a genuine dispute of material fact. See FED. R. CIV. PROC. 56(a). To survive a motion for

 summary judgment, the non-moving party must provide admissible evidence which

 would allow a reasonable jury to find in his or her favor. See Maclin v. SBC Ameritech, 520

 F.3d 781, 786 (7th Cir. 2008). Generally, the Court’s role is to determine whether a genuine

 issue of material fact exists rather than evaluate the weight of the evidence, judge witness

 credibility, or determine the truth of the matter when determining the outcome of such a

 motion. See National Athletic Sportswear, Inc. v. Westfield Ins. Co., 528 F.3d 508, 512 (7th Cir.

 2008).

          However, in Pavey v. Conley, the Seventh Circuit held that, “debatable factual

 issues relating to the defense of failure to exhaust administrative remedies” are not

 required to be decided by a jury but are to be determined by the judge. 544 F.3d 739, 740-

                                            Page 4 of 8
 Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS        Document 64         Filed 08/14/26   Page 5 of 8   Page ID #151




 741 (7th Cir. 2008). Therefore, the Court must determine whether an inmate has

 exhausted his or her remedies when the affirmative defense of non-exhaustion is raised.

 If the court finds that the inmate failed to exhaust administrative remedies, then the

 inmate is given the opportunity to exhaust should time still permit or if the failure to

 exhaust was innocent. Id. at 742. If the court determines that the failure to exhaust was

 the inmate’s fault, then the case is over. Id.

        Under the Prison Litigation Reform Act (“PLRA”), which governs lawsuits filed

 by inmates, “no action shall be brought with respect to prison conditions under § 1983 of

 this title, or any other Federal Law, by a prisoner confined in any jail, prison, or other

 correctional facility until such administrative remedies as are available are exhausted.”

 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a). This coincides with the PLRA’s statutory purpose of “afford[ing]

 correction officials [the] time and opportunity to address complaints internally before

 allowing the initiation of a federal case.” Woodford v. Ngo, 548 U.S. 81, 93 (2006); see also

 Begolli v. Home Depot U.S.A., Inc., 701 F.3d 1158, 1161 (7th Cir. 2012). It affords prison

 administrators an opportunity to fix the problem, reduce damages, and shed light on the

 factual disputes that may arise in litigation. See Pozo v. McCaughtry, 286 F.3d 1022, 1023-

 24 (7th Cir. 2002).

        Inmates must follow their prison’s administrative rules when attempting to

 exhaust administrative remedies under the PLRA. See Pozo, 286 F.3d at 1023. Hackethal

 is an inmate in the IDOC and is required to follow the regulations contained in the IDOC’s

 Grievance Procedures to exhaust his claims. See 20 ILL. ADMIN. CODE § 504.800, et seq. The

 Seventh Circuit requires strict adherence to a prison’s grievance procedures to satisfy the

                                           Page 5 of 8
 Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS       Document 64       Filed 08/14/26    Page 6 of 8     Page ID #152




 requirements for exhaustion under the PLRA. See Dole v. Chandler, 438 F.3d 804, 809 (7th

 Cir. 2006). The exhaustion requirement cannot be satisfied if an inmate files untimely or

 procedurally defective grievances. See Woodford, 548 U.S. at 83. Additionally, an inmate

 must correctly complete all the steps outlined in the grievance procedures and is barred

 from filing suit prior to any step being completed. See Ford v. Johnson, 362 F.3d 395, 398

 (7th Cir. 2004); 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a). If an inmate fails to complete all the steps correctly

 to exhaust his claim, then “the prison administrative authority can refuse to hear the case,

 and the prisoner’s claim can be indefinitely unexhausted.” Dole, 438 F.3d at 809. However,

 inmates are not required to exhaust administrative remedies that are unavailable to them

 which can occur if, “prison employees do not respond to a properly filed grievance or

 otherwise use affirmative misconduct to prevent a prisoner from exhausting.” Dole, 438

 F.3d at 809.

        The IDOC Grievance Procedures require that an inmate first file a grievance with

 a counselor at their correctional institution within 60 days of the discovery of an incident.

 See 20 ILL. ADMIN. CODE § 504.810(a). The Grievance must include, “factual details

 regarding each aspect of the offender’s complaint, including what happened, when,

 where and the name of each person who is the subject of or who is otherwise involved in

 the complaint.” See 20 ILL. ADMIN. CODE § 504.810(c). If the inmate is unsatisfied with the

 counselor’s response, then the inmate can submit a formal grievance to the prison’s

 grievance officer. Id. at (a)-(b). The grievance officer must then review the grievance and

 provide a written response to the inmate. See 20 ILL. ADMIN. CODE § 504.830(a). Within 60

 days of the receipt of the grievance, the grievance officer must report their findings and

                                         Page 6 of 8
 Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS         Document 64       Filed 08/14/26     Page 7 of 8     Page ID #153




 recommendations in writing to the CAO. See 20 ILL. ADMIN. CODE § 504.830(e). The CAO

 will then review the findings and recommendations and offer a written decision to the

 inmate. Id. The inmate can appeal the CAO’s decision to the ARB within 30 days. See 20

 ILL. ADMIN. CODE § 504.850(a). To do this correctly, the inmate is required to attach copies

 of the grievance officer’s report and the CAO’s decision to his appeal. Id. The ARB then

 submits its findings and recommendations to the Director who will issue the IDOC’s final

 decision within six months. See 20 ILL. ADMIN. CODE § 504.850(d)-(e).

                                          DISCUSSION

        Defendants are entitled to summary judgment because Plaintiff filed this suit

 before fully exhausting his administrative remedies. Exhaustion of administrative is a

 precondition to filing a suit under the PLRA. See Perez v. Wisconsin Dept. of Corrections,

 182 F.3d 532, 534 (7th Cir. 1999). “A prisoner must exhaust administrative remedies

 before filing suit: a ‘sue first, exhaust later’ approach is not acceptable.” Chambers v. Sood,

 956 F.3d 979, 984 (7th Cir. 2020). See also Perez, 182 F.3d at 535 (stating that “a suit filed by

 a prisoner before administrative remedies have been exhausted must be dismissed; the

 district court lacks discretion to resolve the claim on the merits, even if the prisoner

 exhausts intra-prison remedies before judgment.”).

        Where a prisoner files suit before he has exhausted administrative remedies, the

 case must be dismissed without prejudice. See Chambers, 956 F.3d at 984. The prisoner can

 file a new suit once he has fully exhausted administrative remedies, provided that it is

 possible for him to do so. Id. Here, the record indisputably shows that Plaintiff filed suit

 after appealing his grievance to the ARB, but before the ARB decided the appeal.

                                           Page 7 of 8
 Case 3:25-cv-00414-GCS        Document 64       Filed 08/14/26     Page 8 of 8     Page ID #154




 Plaintiff’s complaint is dated March 27, 2025. (Doc. 1, p. 1). The ARB decision that is

 attached to both the Motion for Summary Judgment and Plaintiff’s response is dated

 April 15, 2025. (Doc. 55-1, p. 2; Doc. 59, p. 4). Plaintiff himself says that he filed this suit

 only three days after the ARB received his appeal. (Doc. 59, p. 1). Because Plaintiff filed

 suit before he had fully exhausted his administrative remedies, Defendants are entitled

 to summary judgment.

                                         CONCLUSION

        For the reasons outlined above, Defendants’ Motion for Summary Judgment is

 GRANTED. (Doc. 55). The Court DISMISSES the case without prejudice.

        IT IS SO ORDERED.

        DATED: August 14, 2026.                                    Digitally signed by
                                                                   Judge Sison

                         IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

 MOHAMED R. AL-‘OWHALI,                           )
                                                  )
                                   Plaintiff,     )

 vs.                                              )         Civil No. 3:25-cv-235-NJR
                                                  )
 DANIEL SPROUL and J. HUGHES,                     )
                                                  )
                                   Defendants.    )

        NOTICE TO PRO SE PLAINTIFF OF CONSEQUENCES OF FAILING TO
       RESPOND TO THE DEFENDANTS’ MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT

        Defendants, by and through their attorneys, Steven D. Weinhoeft, United States Attorney

 for the Southern District of Illinois, and Kyle Christopher Oehmke, Assistant United States

 Attorney, submit this notice to pro se Plaintiff of consequences of failing to respond to Defendants’

 Motion for Summary Judgment pursuant to Rule 56 against Plaintiff.

        Defendants hereby give notice to the pro se Plaintiff, Mohamed R. Al’-Owhali, that the

 Court may take as true any facts alleged in Defendants’ Motion, which is supported by declaration

 and documentary evidence, unless Plaintiff contradicts those facts with material evidence. If

 Plaintiff fails to contradict the facts alleged by Defendants, the Court may grant judgment in favor

 of Defendants and grant the relief requested.

         Rule 56 provides, in relevant part:

         (a) Motion for Summary Judgment or Partial Summary Judgment. A party
         may move for summary judgment, identifying each claim or defense—or the part
         of each claim or defense—on which summary judgment is sought. The court
         shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine
         dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter
         of law. The court should state on the record the reasons for granting or denying
         the motion.

                                                      ***
         (c) Procedures.
 Case 3:25-cv-00235-NJR       Document 28        Filed 04/07/26      Page 2 of 4       Page ID #270




               (1) Supporting Factual Positions. A party asserting that a fact cannot
               be or is genuinely disputed must support the assertion by:

                       (A) citing to particular parts of materials in the record, including
                       depositions, documents, electronically stored information,
                       affidavits or declarations, stipulations (including those made for
                       purposes of the motion only), admissions, interrogatory answers,
                       or other materials; or

                       (B) showing that the materials cited do not establish the absence
                       or presence of a genuine dispute, or that an adverse party cannot
                       produce admissible evidence to support the fact.

               (2) Objection That a Fact Is Not Supported by Admissible Evidence.
               A party may object that the material cited to support or dispute a fact
               cannot be presented in a form that would be admissible in evidence.

               (3) Materials Not Cited. The court need consider only the cited
               materials, but it may consider other materials in the record.

               (4) Affidavits or Declarations. An affidavit or declaration used to
               support or oppose a motion must be made on personal knowledge, set out
               facts that would be admissible in evidence, and show that the affiant or
               declarant is competent to testify on the matters stated.

                                              ***

        (e) Failing to Properly Support or Address a Fact. If a party fails to properly
        support an assertion of fact or fails to properly address another party’s assertion
        of fact as required by Rule 56(c), the court may:

               (1)     give an opportunity to properly support or address the fact;

                       including the facts considered undisputed – show that the movant
